analysis.one_liner: Lets workers and others take race discrimination claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 12 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often require workers and consumers to sign agreements before any dispute arises that force them to settle complaints in private arbitration instead of court, and to give up joining group cases. This bill would let a person alleging race, color, or national-origin discrimination or harassment choose to go to court anyway, and a judge, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the rule applies. The bill was introduced by Sen. Cory Booker and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, tenants, borrowers, and consumers who face race, color, or national-origin discrimination and would get the choice to have their case heard by a judge rather than a private arbitrator. People alleging retaliation or harassment on those grounds, and members of class or collective actions, also benefit. Workers who are Black, Hispanic, or otherwise more likely to face discrimination claims are the main group affected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers facing race discrimination

how_it_helps.text: At the election of the person alleging discrimination, harassment, or retaliation on the basis of race, color, or national origin, a predispute arbitration agreement and a predispute ban on group lawsuits would be invalid and unenforceable for that case.
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the bill applies, so the party with the arbitration clause could not have that question sent back to the arbitrator.
It would apply to claims under federal, Tribal, state, or local law, and to any dispute arising after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and other companies that use pre-employment or consumer arbitration clauses would lose a tool for keeping discrimination disputes out of court, where cases are public, slower, and potentially costlier, and where juries can award larger verdicts. Private arbitration providers would lose business from this category of disputes.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of arbitration argue it is often faster and cheaper for individual workers than a years-long court case, and the bill would take away that option for the worker's own dispute category without requiring the worker to prove arbitration was worse.

The bill covers only race, color, and national origin. Congress already barred forced arbitration for sexual assault and sexual harassment claims in 2022, so this bill adds one more category rather than a single consistent rule, leaving a patchwork of protections by claim type.
Cases moved from arbitration into court take longer and cost more to litigate, which can itself deter workers with weaker claims or smaller damages from pursuing them at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people facing race discrimination, the ability to choose a public court with a judge and jury instead of a private arbitrator selected under a contract they did not negotiate is a meaningful right, and the bill deliberately leaves the choice in the worker's hands rather than banning arbitration outright. The costs fall on employers through longer, more public, and more expensive disputes, and the main honest criticism is the piecemeal approach: it addresses one category of claim at a time rather than forced arbitration as a whole.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on May 2, 2023, joined by Sens. Gillibrand and Durbin.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that is the last action in the record for the entire two-year Congress.
Twelve senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, and no Senate Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with arbitration clauses and the private arbitration industry, which keep the current system where discrimination claims can be steered into private arbitration.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats and no Senate Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would let discrimination claims escape private arbitration into public court, where verdicts are larger and proceedings are public. Keeping those claims in arbitration keeps outcomes confidential and typically cheaper for the company. If the bill dies, this status quo continues. If the bill had passed, employers would bear longer, costlier, more public disputes.
Arbitration firms and their panels are paid to hear the disputes that companies' contracts channel to them. A category of cases workers could pull out of arbitration would shrink that business.
